newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOCCER-CORRUPTION HAUNTS SOUTH AFRICAN SOCCER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CORRUPTION HAUNTS SOUTH AFRICAN SOCCER.

text.p: South African soccer success after decades of isolation has contrasted starkly with tales of deep intrigue in the administration of the country's favourite sport.

While South Africa have won the African Nations' Cup and moved into the top 20 of the FIFA rankings after just four years back on the world stage, revelations of corruption and farcical on-field incidents have threatened to retard this remarkable progress after almost 30 years of apartheid-enforced isolation.

Details of administrative corruption, allegations of a poisioning plot, a $10 million lawsuit served on a journalist and a top league match where just 10 players from the one team turned up, are among recent events which cloud South Africa's forthcoming World Cup qualifiers.
A judical commission into the affairs of the South African Football Association has heard that the association's executive president Solomon Morewa has been involved in financial irregularities.

Morewa has admitted to the commission, appointed by sports minister Steve Tshwete after press allegations of corruption, that he accepted an interest-free loan of more than $100,000 from the marketing company appointed to run Safa's affairs.

He has also admitted taking money from a special fund set up to help soccer players seeking to finance their tertiary education. Other leading administrators had also been given "grants" from the fund.
South African newspapers called for Morewa's resignation at the weekend after it was revealed that he had attacked a journalist covering the commission's hearings in Johannesburg.

Morewa, who last year formed part of world governing body FIFA's inspection team to Japan and South Korea ahead of the annoucement of the World Cup finals venue for 2002, forms part of the so-called "A team". The group comprises powerful sports officials, club owners and prominent black businessmen who wear expensive Italian suits and entertain lavishly at top restaurants.
The "A-team" have locked in a bitter power struggle with members of the so-called "B-team", made up of club owners critical of the power wheeled by their rivals.

"A-team" member Kaizer Motaung, owner of the country's best known club Kaizer Chiefs, alleged he had stayed away from the launch of the new professional Premier Soccer League in August after being tipped off that an attempt was being planned to poison him by spiking the cocktails and snacks on offer at the function.
A high-level police investigation has since been launched into Motaung's claims.

The Premier Soccer League, administered by Englishman Trevor Phillips who left the Football Association in London earlier this year under a cloud of controversy following European championship ticket allocations, has made a spluttering start.
Last month, players of Witbank Aces went on strike ahead of their match against league leaders Kaizer Chiefs, leaving just 10 of the team, including two goalkeepers, to take the field.
Aces lost 7-2 despite their assistant coach scoring the goal of the game.

Earlier this month, Safa's marketing agents, Awesome Sports International, filed a 45 million rand ($9.5 million) defamation suit against sports reporter Thomas Kwenaite, author of the initial allegations of malpractice in the soccer administration.
Kwenaite was also given a police bodyguard after alleging he had received death threats.
Corruption is not new in South African soccer. Two top officials were jailed four years ago after defrauding the league of some 7.4 million rand ($1.56 million).
Against this backdrop national coach Clive Barker has been preparing for South Africa's attempt to qualify for a first World Cup finals appearance.
The controversies have had remarkably little impact on a team who have lost just two of their last 25 matches and are highly fancied to go to France in 1998.
South Africa open their final round group three campaign with a November 9 fixture against Zaire at Johannesburg's Soccer City.
